AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEFINITION OF CONTRACT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: for leave to introduce a bill entitled an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEFINITION OF CONTRACT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING DEFINITION OF CONTRACT OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to insert in the Unemployment Insurance Act the definition of the words "employee" and "employer" and, through the use of more general terms, to place the service contract and the rental of work in the category of insurable employment.
These amendments are being suggested in order to clarify and facilitate the interpretation of the act by making it more consistent with the intention of parliament when this legislation was passed in 1955.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26
for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the displacement of 160 employees-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I am just wondering whether his request would properly be made now. The rule says at the end of routine proceedings. I find that the hon. member is quite correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. My motion to adjourn the house is for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the displacement of 160 employees of the Canadian National Railways at the main office on McGill street in Montreal through the substitution of contract labour, which appears to be part of a national pattern affecting employees of the Canadian National Railways across Canada. I would hope that Your Honour would give me permission to establish urgency in this case.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I shall be glad to hear the hon. member. I assume that it is a matter of importance, but the urgency that is involved is urgency of debate. I think I should like to hear the hon. member on the question of whether or not this is one of the administrative responsibilities of the ministry. It seems to me that the point may well be taken that it is a decision, of the Canadian National Railways on its own authority.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall be glad to deal with those three points if the house will bear with me. Dealing first with the urgency of the matter, I should tell Your Honour that over the week end I received an urgent communication from the brotherhood of railway carmen of America, signed by the local chairman of Lodge 733, Mr. G. Gagnon, and by the president, Mr. H. Myer-son.
In this communication two points among many others are made. The first is that these employees are gravely concerned about the announced intention of the Canadian National Railways in the Montreal area to effect layoffs and dismissals of the maintenance and cleaning personnel in the Montreal headquarters building coincidental with the sale of the building at 360 McGill street and the occupancy of the new office building adjacent to the Canadian National Railways station. It is pointed out in this communication that

Canadian National Railways 160 employees are affected, and that unless something is done to stop the contract which is about to be given, if it has not already been given, for the new office building adjacent to the C.N.R. station their position will be an untenable one. It is pointed out that most of the people affected by the decision will be unable to find jobs elsewhere because of their age. They are for the most part over 40 years of age, and the majority of those affected are widows who are the sole support of their children.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. If I may interrupt the hon. member. I think he need not labour the point as to the importance of the matter. The question is really one of urgency of debate. I take it that this decision has been made since the estimates of the Department of Labour were under discussion here last Friday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, sir.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Therefore it is a matter which has arisen since then. The hon. member might direct his attention to the possibility for debate of this matter in the ordinary course of events, rather than interrupting the proceedings of the house. The other point-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have not forgotten the other point, sir. We are dealing with urgency of debate, and Your Honour is quite familiar with the position in so far as discussion in the house is concerned. First there are the labour estimates under which this matter could ostensibly be discussed. The labour estimates have not been called this week and I presume they will not be called, in view of the information which was given on Thursday of last week. Nothing on the order paper indicates, therefore, that there is any possibility of discussing this matter under the labour estimates.
The next point is that the only other place where the matter can be discussed, if at all, is in the committee on railways, air lines and shipping owned and operated by the government. I think the Minister of Transport has indicated in the house that this committee will not sit until after the Easter recess. In any event, it has not been set up yet. As Your Honour knows, I attempted in a general way to deal with this matter on the establishment of the committee on railways, air lines and shipping, and my attention was drawn to the fact that while I could refer to lay-offs in a general way, I was not to go into the matter in detail. I did take exception to that ruling; none the less that seemed to be the decision. So there will not be any opportunity of discussing a matter of this nature until well after the Easter recess.


Your Honour was quite right a moment ago in saying that this matter has arisen within the last day or so. It arose over the week end when the matter has been brought to our attention. Those are the two points that I make with reference to urgency of debate. There will be no opportunity from now until after the Easter recess to deal with the matter.
The third point which Your Honour has asked me to deal with concerns the administrative responsibility of the government. It seems to me that if this matter is not allowed under that heading, then it must of necessity follow that no matter affecting a crown corporation could be discussed under the heading of administrative responsibility of the government. Surely that is not the manner in which the rules have been applied. For instance, if a matter concerned the national harbours board or any other crown corporation, it could well be stated that this was not the administrative responsibility of the government.
I say to you, sir, that it is because, first, the responsibility must rest with the minister whose duty it is to answer for the Canadian National Railways in the House of Commons. Next, it is the government of Canada which owns the shares, on behalf of the people of Canada, of the Canadian National Railways. Third, the government itself is the owner of a number of railways, such as the Intercolonial and, I believe, the Hudson Bay Railway.
Thus I say, sir, with deference that under these three heads the rules allow us to discuss this matter. I should also like to add an additional reason, namely that this is national in its scope. While I have dealt so far only with the situation in Montreal, I have before me here evidence of a pattern which is similar in many other areas, particularly in the three districts affected by this action as they were known before reorganization, namely the eastern district, the central district and the western district where there have been lay-offs amounting to about 6 per cent per year in the staff and personnel of the railway.
There is one final point I should like to make. I think Your Honour has held on one or two occasions in the past that in discussing matters of this kind it is essential to establish not only that the motion be national in scope but that there be a certain confusion existing. My point is this: Thus far the government has indicated no intention on its part of telling the house what these layoffs have amounted to, and in that respect there has been little or no information-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I think that point is one which might arise if the hon. member is given leave, but not otherwise.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I wonder if I might say a word on the question of urgency.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Laurier permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Did the letter which the hon. member referred to bear a Montreal postmark or a Chicago postmark?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Unfortunately I have not the envelope here but my memory is quite clear. It came from Montreal and not from Chicago. There is no doubt about that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Perhaps, while the hon.
member is referring to the letter, he would tell me the date of the letter?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes. The date is March 9, and it is from the office of the local chairman of lodge No. 703, brotherhood of railway carmen of America, and he is Mr. G. Gagnon, of 4477 Bourbonniere street, Montreal. May I complete my answer to that question. The question has been asked, when did I receive the letter? I received the letter by special delivery on Sunday afternoon.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that this is a Canadian matter, which seems to be an inference that might be taken from the question which has been raised. I have received a letter from the same organization and bearing the same signatures. For your benefit, Mr. Speaker, I may say I have also received a telegram dated Montreal, Quebec, March 10.
As to the question of the administrative responsibility of the government, I think the very fact that the president of the C.N.R. is brought before a committee of this house from year to year at the time when C.N.R. matters are discussed establishes beyond question that parliament itself can deal with important questions of C.N.R. administration.
As has already been pointed out, there is urgency attaching to such a debate because there will not be an occasion on which this question can be raised in the foreseeable future. I also submit this is an indication of a general pattern which has arisen across the country, namely that the C.N.R. is engaged in wholesale lay-offs that are adding to unemployment problems in the country and creating growing hardship among the people who have been dismissed.
I join with the hon. member for Laurier in submitting that this is a matter of urgent public importance. It is essential that it be dealt with and debated by parliament. It is certainly within the administrative competence of the government, and surely it is
Canadian National Railways within the power of parliament to deal with general questions relating to the Canadian National Railways.
Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that very careful consideration should be given to an attempt to adjourn the house such as the motion moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Laurier. Let us look at the situation. It appears to boil down to a case of a wire being sent to the hon. members for Laurier and Assiniboia by two men who happen to be officers of a union, and on the basis of that wire these two hon. members rise in the house and insist that we should abandon our plans for discussing public business today in order to consider the wire which has been sent in this manner.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: To consider a matter of urgent public importance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Let the hon. member be silent and take his medicine. Surely the rule under which this motion is moved was never designed to meet a situation of this type. This procedure is supposed to be used only on rare occasions when there is a necessity and great urgency for debate. In years past motions to adjourn the house have not been accepted on more than perhaps two or three occasions in a session. Because the hon. member succeeded in getting away with another motion two weeks ago-

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: -or rather succeeded in having a similar motion accepted two weeks ago-

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: A reflection on Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I withdrew the words "got away with". In view of the success of hon. members opposite in having a similar motion accepted two weeks ago, I presume because this Monday is set aside for the discussion of private members' business they decided to make this attempt.
From time to time men are laid off. We all regret that. Members of the government do their best to avoid that happening. On every occasion when this happens are we to be faced with a motion to adjourn the house to discuss it for the rest of the day? This, I suggest, would be reducing to an absolute mockery the rules for the conduct of business in this house. I suggest that today is a good time to put a stop to attempts of this kind.
There is on today's order paper under "Government Business" item No. 9, a resolution for the setting up of a committee to consider the affairs of Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines. That motion has already been under discussion on one occasion within the last few days, and I

Canadian National Railways have no doubt it will be called again within the next few days. Discussion under that order of business will give ample opportunity to the hon. member for Laurier to raise the point which he seeks to raise today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question? Is he aware of the ruling of the chair in connection with these matters, that a member may not go into detail so far as lay-offs on the C.N.R. are concerned but may discuss them in a general way only?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I was not here at the time any such ruling was made, but the hon. member for Laurier has tried to broaden his motion in his remarks. He has tried to lay a basis or foundation encompassing the treatment of employees by the C.N.R. generally, and certainly that matter would be in order on a motion to set up the committee.
Another point is that questions such as these do not come directly under any minister, and nobody should know that better than the hon. member for Laurier-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is not so.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
-because he was minister of transport for several years. Time after time when he was asked a question about the Canadian National Railways I have heard him get up in the house and say that he had to consult the president or other officials of the railway and that he could not possibly give an answer until he had done so. Today he has forgotten all about that and he comes here and expects us to deal with some administrative action by the officials of the Canadian National Railways without any opportunity to consult them. Oh, no; today the C.N.R. is entirely the responsibility of the government. There is no question today of the C.N.R. being a corporation operating on its own. This shows what a ridiculous attempt is being made today by the hon. member for Laurier.
In addition to the motion to set up the committee there is to be a supply motion a week from today, and the hon. member for Laurier and his pal from Assiniboia-it is very significant how as soon as one of them makes such a motion the other rushes to get on the band wagon and, of course, that has been done today-will then have the opportunity, either alone or in combination again, to move a motion of want of confidence in the government on this issue, but by that time they will be frying other fish; they will have forgotten all about this particular problem. There will be that opportunity a week from today, however, and I suggest that if we do not take the whole of today to talk about a wire which has been received signed by two individuals the whole process of democracy


will not be upset. I suggest this is a lot of foolishness, and that this motion should not be accepted.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I feel that I have heard
enough from the hon. members to permit me to deal with the matter unless the hon. member for Laurier wishes to reply to some specific point made by the Acting Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If I may be allowed I should like to do so. There are two or three specific points to which I should like to reply and I will do so as quickly as I can. The main point is that the Acting Prime Minister has made it quite clear, I think, that there is an administrative responsibility on the part of the government because his whole argument in reply to mine left no other impression. He implied, for instance, that this matter should be taken up on a motion to go into supply which will not be until next Monday if the government so announces this as business for Monday, or in the alternative on the motion for the establishment of the committee on railways and shipping owned and operated by the government. So far as the latter suggestion is concerned, the Speaker and Deputy Speaker have already ruled clearly that the matter cannot be discussed then. The Acting Prime Minister also stated that this matter does not come under any minister.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I did not say that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I took down the words used by the Acting Prime Minister and he said that this matter did not come under any minister. There is a responsibility on the Minister of Transport to report to the house on matters affecting the Canadian National Railways. That has always been the case. It was the case when I was over there, just as it is now, and under that head it seems to me there is a responsibility on the part of the government.
The minister then asked whether every time such an event happens the government is to be faced with a motion such as the one now made. I suggest this is the first time such a motion has been made, and it has been moved not only because of what is happening in Montreal but because of the evidence I have here indicating that the same thing is happening in other parts of the country, in the west, in the central section, in Lauzon, in Moncton. As the whip says, it is happening everywhere that the C.N.R. has jurisdiction, as I will be able to establish if the opportunity is given to adjourn the house.
The final statement made by the Acting Prime Minister was that this motion was being moved because a couple of wires had been received. I did not receive any wire. I

made it quite clear that I got a special communication which came to me on Sunday afternoon. It is because of that communication that I consider this matter is urgent and have brought it to the attention of the house.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Stormont supporting the request for leave?

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Surely-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. If the hon. member for Stormont is supporting the request for leave I will hear him; otherwise not.

subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Indeed not, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LAY-OFFS OF PERSONNEL, MONTREAL    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Laurier, as he is entitled to do, has asked under standing order 26 for leave to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance. Each of these requests must, of course, be dealt with on its own facts, and I do not have much difficulty in arriving at the conclusion that this is not a case where leave should be given.
In support of my view I remind the house that this is the sixth private members' Monday, and that to interrupt our ordinary proceedings there should be a clear case which warrants the setting aside of the planned business of the day because this is the last opportunity of this kind which private members will have to discuss their bills and motions. As I say, the case should be a clear one.
I raise the question of administrative responsibility. May I put the facts this way as I see them. First, I should say I am not clear whether the 160 employees referred to by the hon. member for Laurier have been laid off or whether there is a threat or a notice of intention to lay them off, but for my purposes it does not really make any difference. The problem of their employment is, of course, an important matter to them at least and of significance to the Montreal area. However, parliament has given to the Canadian National Railways the responsibility for administering the railway and included in administration is the responsibility for all labour policy. It is true that parliament can change the legislation but it is not true, as I see it, that the government can intervene to direct Canadian National Railways to do something different.
As hon. members will recall, the matter of lay-offs of employees of the Canadian National Railways arises very frequently during the question period, and the minister is always under the necessity of having to say that he will inquire from the C.N.R. to find
Motions for Papers
out what their policy is and that he will bring back an answer to the house. It seems to me that citation 100, which indicates that such matters should relate to the administrative responsibility of the government, might be applied in this case in the sense that the responsibility is indirectly through parliament and not one on which a debate on a motion of this kind could have any direct effect or result. It would be necessary for parliament to amend its Canadian National Railways legislation, if an enforceable decision is to be made or an effective remedy applied.
That may not appeal to all hon. members as a correct summary of the situation, but in addition to that point I think that lay-offs of this kind, whether isolated or part of a pattern, are a continuing problem of employees of the government owned railway which will be coming before the house from time to time when it is sitting, and should be dealt with on the occasions on which it is possible to debate the administrative policies of the Canadian National Railways and the control of these policies by parliament.
I therefore regretfully have to refuse the hon. member leave.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext: If you will recall, Mr. Speaker, this motion was to stand until the return of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext: I remember that the last time this motion was called the Acting Prime Minister suggested that it be dropped from the order paper and I rather resisted that action in the belief that it had been the practice not to drop motions in the absence of the mover. But I find that he is correct, in accordance with standing order 19, and that unless the government requests that a notice of motion shall stand when it is called, it is dropped. maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext:
On this point, Mr. Speaker, I endeavoured to review the rules and the practice in the past. Although perhaps this is not a matter of very great moment, nevertheless I think some ruling from the Chair might be helpful for the future.
As we all know, these motions are not debatable. Therefore the presence of the hon. member who has put the motion on the order paper is not absolutely essential. The hon. member is looking for information, and that information is either given or denied by the minister responsible.
In the past the practice has been to permit someone else to move the motion in the absence of the proposer. That was done on March 6. Quite correctly, Mr. Speaker, when the request was made that the motion be withdrawn you stated that this could not
Motions for Papers
be done without the hon. member being present. That is in accordance with standing order 49, which says:
A member who has made a motion may withdraw the same only by the unanimous consent of the house.
However, on looking back in Bourinot's fourth edition on page 300, which deals with-

maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext: If you are referring to Bourinot you are going a long way back.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext:
I point out to the hon. member who has interrupted that Beauchesne was founded on Bourinot, and Bourinot's rules still carry authority in the House of Commons. Bourinot deals at very great length with this subject and Beauchesne does not. I think the reason Beauchesne does not deal with the subject of motions for production of papers is that the method of procedure had been so well established that the author thought it was not necessary to refer to it.
On page 300 of Bourinot, dealing with this type of motion, it says:
Neither can any motion be withdrawn in the absence of the member who proposed it; but it may be negatived or agreed to in such a case on the question being put formally from the chair.
Then Bourinot gives an example of where that was done; the mover of the motion was absent but the matter was disposed of. In this particular instance the Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated that the motion is not acceptable. Therefore it is not a question of the hon. member having the privilege of withdrawing, which requires unanimous consent, but simply of disposing of it immediately. It could be put before us by one of his colleagues and then it would be in the hands of the house and we could either accept or reject it as we saw fit; otherwise it stands on the order paper. I think that is unnecessary, particularly in view of the fact that on this question of motions for production of papers there is a sentence in standing order 47 which reads:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of-
It seems to me that our practice has been to dispose of them except on the request of the government that the motion shall stand for some special consideration, as is the case with order No. 50 on our order paper.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR
speechtext:
I think the practice has perhaps developed by consent somewhat divergently from the express wording of the rule. Standing order 47, which deals with notices of motions for the production of papers, provides as follows:
All such notices when called shall be forthwith disposed of-

Motions for Papers
That has already been indicated by the minister. That means they are not debatable. Standing order 47 continues:
-but If on any such motion a debate be desired, it will be transferred by the clerk to the order of ''Notices of motions".
That is the special rule relating to this particular type of notice. Then standing order 19 (1), to which I referred previously, says:
Questions put by members and notices of motions, not taken up when called may (upon the requests of the government) be allowed to stand and retain their precedence; otherwise they will disappear from the order paper. They may, however, be renewed.
I think that amendment, when it was introduced to the rules, was intended to prevent the accumulation on the order paper of notices which, if dropped, were not prejudiced in any way. As I see the matter now, unless the government asks that the motion stand or the house accepts a motion on behalf of the absent member so that the question could be voted upon, the rule would require the motion to be dropped.

maintopic: EVACUATION PRIORITIES IN EVENT OF NUCLEAR WAR

On clause 1-Incorporation.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a very few minutes to say a few words on clause 1 of Bill No. S-9, to incorporate international brain research organization.
Without doubt this is an important measure. We were given a most interesting discourse on the bill by the sponsor when the motion for second reading was before the house. In no way whatsoever am I opposing the bill, but I do feel it raises one or two questions with respect to which I should like to have the comments of the sponsor.
The purport of the bill in principle is to incorporate the international brain research

Private Bills
organization tor the purposes outlined in the objects set forth in the bill. To be precise, those objects are to develop, support, coordinate, promote and undertake throughout the world scientific research and education in all fields concerning the brain, to promote international collaboration and interchange of scientific information on brain research, and to provide and assist in the dissemination of information relating to brain research through any media whatsoever.
In so far as brain research is concerned, I feel it is very important to attempt to understand just what drives an individual, although it is a very difficult problem in view of the fact that almost everyone has an aberration of one kind or another. I should like to hear some comment from the hon. member, who is sponsoring this bill, regarding the research attack on the problem of finding out what is wrong with the mind, and why it is perhaps necessary to establish this additional organization for that particular job.
We all appreciate that there are innumerable associations and organizations, provincial, national and international, which deal with different aspects of research on the human body in attempts to find causes and cures. There are associations in existence today which deal with diseases of the heart and chest, as well as cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and arteriosclerosis. There are of course additional organizations dealing with research regarding both children's diseases and mental health problems. I have only named a few.
In view of the fact that the sponsor of this bill has a magnificent reputation not only as a member of this house but as a physician and surgeon, and in view of his interest in research, I would ask that during the introduction of this bill to incorporate a brain research organization he satisfy us of the existence of some of the problems in this connection. He could perhaps indicate whether he thinks the time has arrived, in regard to research of this type, when an over-all organization should be established. We all know that hardly a two week period passes without our receiving analytical reports from various organizations of this kind. During the same period individuals receive requests to join, make donations and, in general, help these organizations in some way. We all realize that these organizations hold individual drives and community drives in attempts to raise funds.
I would ask the sponsor of this bill to indicate, as I have said earlier, in view of the existence of these various organizations and the legislation both provincial and national which covers them, whether an

over-all research body should be established to support the research in respect of these various diseases. I am sure that if these organizations continue attempting to support research in the way they have in the past, we will reach the point where we will be asked to establish an organization to support research into the problems of hangnails and dandruff. I appreciate of course that this is an exaggeration, but I hope the sponsor will appreciate the point I am making. I feel that now is the time for the hon. member sponsoring this bill to express himself about the entire medical research situation and the method of financing research programs. I would certainly appreciate it if the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa would rise at this time and expatiate, as my chemistry teacher used to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Before the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa replies I would say that if he follows the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East he will open the door to a wide debate. We might find that we are discussing the whole problem of research, and we are now at the committee stage of this bill, with the sole object of incorporating the international brain research organization. I have no objection to the hon. member making a short reply but I would warn him that I might be forced to intervene if the debate becomes too wide.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member for Vancouver East seems to be puzzled by the number of organizations for research into cancer, heart disease, arteriosclerosis, but I must remind him that these are national research organizations and that the proposed organization is an international research organization respecting brain research. Despite the fact that we have quite extensive research in this country it is fairly localized to two or three spots in Canada and therefore confined. We find, as a result, that most of our discoveries in connection with the brain have been made only in the past 15 or 20 years and have come to light in the main through international meetings which have not been organized, except by research teams from different countries.
At the meeting where this suggestion concerning an international organization was made there were 247 members in attendance. These individuals were not general practitioners or surgeons, but research men who were very much interested in research in respect of the brain. The organization which is now being proposed has that international flavour which is required because of the fact that the different panels and different disciplines throughout the different countries of

the world use different methods for research into the brain, and to expect them to carry on this very vital task with the support of one country would be too much to ask. That is why this research organization must be set up.
In so far as the questions of development, support and co-ordination are concerned, I might say that proposals have been extensive but will not be accepted until certain funds are provided. This organization will be a clearing house for information at the outset and, following funds being made available through grants from foundations or grants from UNESCO-one has already been received to assist during this formative stage- the organization will be responsible for the establishing of fellowships to assist scientific workers; for the fostering of medical students who are primarily interested in research; and for setting up temporary research teams in countries where funds do not exist to cover the cost of equipment needed for research in respect of brain diseases.
Through their teachers and many of their finest men in this organization they will be available to promote education in brain research. Through the use of laboratory facilities in some of the larger centres of countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, the U.S.S.R. and Canada they will make available the apparatus to help underdeveloped countries in their brain research. I hope that answers the hon. member's question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I want to congratulate the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa on the presentation he made on the motion for second reading of this bill. It seems to me that the hon. member must be a highly trained and qualified doctor. Certainly he has done a good deal of research into the reasoning behind the setting up of this international brain research organization. If a number of our doctors in Canada are as qualified to speak on this subject as he has indicated that he is, I think we in Canada will feel proud of the developments that will take place through the leadership of the members that have been suggested as the founding members of this unincorporated association.
The hon. member points out that there were 250 scientists from 30 countries taking part in the convention held under UNESCO which decided to set up this international organization. They held a central meeting. A number of them were polled and a vote was taken which resulted in the setting up of this organization.
In his introduction the hon. member also pointed out that research of a similar and quite often parallel nature was taking place
Private Bills
in brain research in various countries throughout the world. He mentioned particularly the United States and Russia who, of course, have pioneered in this field along with Britain and Canada under Dr. Penfield himself. He mentioned that these people in many cases had been developing techniques and doing research of a similar nature, and that if the exchange of information and of the equipment that is necessary for this type of work had been available, and the results of that research had been available, probably the duplication that was taking place would have been avoided and the intelligence of doctors experimenting in these fields would have been directed forward rather than running parallel as it now must.
I was very much interested in reading the names of the various people comprising the original committee or association. The first one mentioned is Herbert Henri Jasper, professor, who is widely known for his work and his teaching in the field of brain development. The next is Wilder Graves Penfield, surgeon, who also is very well known. He has been known for many years as an outstanding brain surgeon in the city of Montreal in the Royal Victoria Hospital.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: Montreal Neurological Institute.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
He is a man about whom many stories are told, I can remember one about a young boy being brought down from northern Quebec with a serious brain injury as a result of an accident. When the operation was over and the young lad was on his way to recovery the father, on asking Doctor Penfield how much the bill was going to be, was asked by the doctor how much money he made, and what kind of job he had. When the doctor was informed that the father was a miner in Noranda mine, the bill seemed to have been set in keeping with the earnings of the parent and this young chap was not prevented from receiving the benefit of treatment by this famous doctor. Probably arrangements would be made for the next patient to contribute something toward that assistance.
Brain surgery in Canada, as in other parts of the world, over the years has gone through the same type of reluctant support as that of other forms of medicine from Pasteur and Lister on down. There have always been those who say that you should not play around with things you cannot see, in some cases, and do not understand. It has been a field in which a great deal of difficulty has been experienced when corrective treatment or corrective surgery is attempted; I refer to the field of criminal and psychopathic tendencies. Treatment through the removal or the curtailing of the use of certain lobes in certain

Private Bills
cases may solve the problem with regard to sex deviates and others. A continual cry is going up that this type or research or this type of experimentation should not be allowed. In establishing this international organization it seems to me that we have brought into consideration the facts developed in other countries that probably would have a bearing on the relationship between the legislation and the various types of brain treatment that we would have in Canada as a result of the work done in other countries.
Some countries with more progressive legislation in this field than ours will be a factor, I am quite sure, in the work of the international research organization. I expect it will make it much easier for doctors in Canada and in other countries across the world to do initial research work on the correction of brain ailments. One of the reasons I am interested in the people who were named to the original unincorporated association is the fact that these are the people to whom the people of the world will look for guidance in connection with those who will be suffering or who have suffered from brain injuries.
I looked in the library to see what information was available on some of these people. It is surprising and unfortunate that in many cases more information is not available concerning what has been done and the calibre of the people that we are being asked to endorse in this organization. In the Dalhousie Review I read an article written by one of the doctors involved, namely Dr. Wilder Penfield. He was addressing the Dalhousie University faculty of medicine at their annual refresher course in October 1953 and he said in part as follows:
There is a river not to be found on any map of this terrestrial globe, yet a river well known to all the sons of men, and never very far from any of us. It flows in the Realm of Time. It is Lethe, the river of Oblivion. What memories of noble persons and heroic deeds, what words of wisdom and what glorious thoughts have been engulfed in that dark, remorseless tide.
He was speaking, of course, of research into all facets of brain surgery. He went on to say something that I think most hon. members would be pleased to endorse. He said that in giving these lectures he must wear the mantle of Stewart, who was a former president of that organization. Then he said:
Each doctor of medicine discovers that he wears a cloak of authority and wisdom in the eyes of his patients, if not in the eyes of his family. It covers the nakedness of our shortcomings. It causes us to stand up straight and tall, each one according to the stature God gave him.
The mover of the bill did not say to what extent the organization was going to involve itself in brain research of types other than

those in which it is presently engaged. It has been pointed out by scientists, and it was certainly pointed out by the doctor in the same relationship, that in the science of brain research we have not gone very far. Yet the brain is the fundamental machine which runs the human body and which has developed the human race. It is the machine that gives us those things that are good and in some cases the brain is responsible for those things which are bad. I refer to the malfunctions of the mind that occurred in the late Adolf Hitler. He is certainly not missed by anyone, but pershaps he could have been treated and his undoubted talents could have been put to work in a much better fashion if research in that type of field had been developed to the stage we expect it to develop in the very near future.
Our hospitals in Canada are full of people suffering from mental disorders of one kind or another. Good surgeons will eventually be able to correct a great many of the problems which now affect these people who are in institutions. They have found out exactly what part of the brain produces our faults, controls emotion, memory and the other things that go to make up the human mind. They know that in order to get at these things they have to apply stimulus to the brain. This has only been achieved because of the persistence of people of the calibre of Professor Jasper and Doctor Penfield. If these people, on their own and with very limited resources in many cases, had not been willing to pioneer in this field, particularly in Canada which is a small country with a proportionately small grant for this type of medical development, we would not know what is wrong with a great many of the people who are in our mental institutions.
It seems to me we could gain a great deal from co-operating with countries like Russia, England and the United States and could arrive at a quicker solution to the problem that now exists in Canada. As we look at the statistics of the number of mental patients in hospitals who are under care, we see that this problem is not getting any smaller even though research and surgery facilities have been developed to a great extent. In fact, this problem is getting larger.
The high speed of modern day living, the tensions that are developing at a great rate and the noise factors that are involved, coupled with the lack of exercise and other things that may previously have dissipated some of these tensions, are problems that are being studied in institutions. It has been felt by many people who are concerned with this matter that surgery itself may be a solution for eliminating the tensions that are produced today.

There is another much more positive endeavour, and that is in the field of congenital and pre-natal mental conditions. Many of these conditions are now being prevented by chemistry. Many of the accidents of birth that took place years ago are being prevented by chemistry, the use of hormones and other secretions. These mental ailments are no longer as widespread as they were. A cure is in sight for many of these people born with congenital diseases, and particularly those with submental capacity, through the use of chemical preparations. In the future many more people will be born with normal intelligence, with their minds undamaged, where years ago this was a very large and very worrisome field for doctors. At that time they had no opportunity and no method of checking to find out why this type of development was taking place, or what could be done about it.
I think members of this house are appreciative of the fact that this organization is being born under the auspices of the United Nations, with its support and help, and that it is taking into consideration the best medical research ability that is available. We should be, and are, proud of the fact that this organization is being developed in Canada and that at least for the time being the headquarters of the organization will be in this country.
I think this will mean that those in Canada who are suffering from mental ailments will perhaps in the near future be treated by surgical, chemical and medical methods that will be available here as soon as they are available anywhere else. Probably people across the country will remember these four or five people who are setting up this organization.
As a Canadian I certainly give my wholehearted support to this organization being born and established in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I might be permitted to say a few words on this matter. I believe it was a week ago today, if I am not mistaken, that the miscellaneous private bills committee met and considered this bill. Unfortunately I am not a member of that committee and I was not able to be there. I certainly would have liked to be there because of the extreme importance of the subject matter of the bill itself and the great advantage not only to Canada but to the world that will undoubtedly accrue as a result of the establishment of this organization in this country.
Private Bills
This organization will collect, correlate and disseminate as much information as it possibly can about all the fields and activities of the brain itself. I know that hon. members of this house who are also members of the medical profession have an intense, close concern and interest in the establishment of this organization. Their closeness of concern, of course, comes from their field of work. Those members who are laymen as far as the medical field is concerned have an equal interest though, undoubtedly, their understanding of the complexities of the problem is not as great. So I am sure those hon. members who are directly interested will not think that because some members of this house are, to a degree, inarticulate with regard to this subject they do not take the interest in it which it deserves, because I am sure we all value the importance which this work has in our society. The brain itself is a most fabulous mechanism and though it may sometimes appear to go awry, even the most massive I.B.M. machine must pale into insignificance, I think, compared with some aspects of its activity.
I believe there is little doubt that the house will agree to the passage of this measure, and I wonder if before we pass from this item the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill would explain in a little more detail the financial arrangements of the proposed new organization. He mentioned, I believe, that the United Nations, or UNESCO, had made one financial contribution. I wonder if he could tell the committee what he expects the financial relationship to be between the organization which he now seeks to establish and UNESCO or any similar international organization. Can he tell us whether or not there will be a large financial contribution made by UNESCO, or whether it is hoped that the public will be able to finance this project primarily by means of private contributions.
Before I close I should like to leave this thought with the hon. member. For some time an immediate concern of mine has been the field of narcotic addiction and alcoholism both of which have been considered in recent years, and, I think, correctly so, to be the result of malfunctioning of the mind leading to conduct which is not in accord with that expected by the majority of society. We look upon the results of these addictions as being due to mental disturbances-mental illness- inability to face reality and an attempt to hide from the realities of life. I hope that when the organization is established it will be able to collect and disseminate information in this field concerning the mental functions

Private Bills
of people who have propensities toward addiction to drugs and alcohol to the end that not only here in Canada but in other parts of the world we may have a better understanding of this problem and that we may be able to evolve measures to reduce the waste of human and mental assets to which such addiction leads.

Perhaps I may answer the question concerning financial support. There has been no approach made, as yet, by this unincorporated body, but there has been some agreement in principle, informally, by government research bodies in Canada, France and the United States. The organization has not so far sought any charitable donations. It is hoped that when the bill for incorporation has gone through parliament certain foundations may be approached with a view to their donating money. Since there has been no incorporation as yet, no approach has been made to the Department of National Revenue as to whether or not this is a charitable organization.
To deal with the immediate budget, the estimates are $250,000 a year increasing by that amount over the next three or four years to a final figure of $1 million a year. Thus, hon. members can see that the plans are extensive and require a fair amount of money. As far as the government is concerned, there has been only the contribution made through the national research council of Canada to defray the expenses of the executive secretary, Dr. Jasper, while he was working on the organization of this corporation.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: May I ask the sponsor of this bill if there is any relationship at the present time between this unincorporated organization and the mental health organization which presently operates in Canada. If not, will there be any such relationship in future? At the moment, in the absence of a fuller explanation, I cannot differentiate, generally speaking between the broad aspects of brain research and mental health.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: One is, broadly speaking, engaged in research only and the other is more or less concerned with treatment. The mental health foundation is concerned primarily with the treatment of mental diseases. This corporation is concerned primarily with research.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: On the functions of the brain?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: It will be understood that included in the panels of this organization there are a large number of behavioural scientists who will co-operate with national bodies in any country as far as mental health is concerned.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: This is, then, a straight research organization having to do with the function of the brain and so on. It has nothing to do with diseases of the brain?

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH ORGANIZATION
speechtext: It certainly has. It has very much to do with diseases of the brain. In so far as many aberrations are now considered to be diseases either caused pharmacologically, or by some lesion, chemical lesion or even traumatic lesion of the brain,-all of these have some connection with mental health. But this is a purely research organization. It is not primarily interested in treatment. It is interested in finding out how to treat these cases.

speechtext: Order.

The hon. member for Jasper-Edson has said that the hon. member for Vancouver South made certain statements in this house knowing in advance that the statements he made were incorrect. I would suggest that such an accusation by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson is unparliamentary and should be withdrawn.

If I indeed said what the hon. member for Assiniboia has suggested then I withdraw. What I intended to say was that the hon. member for Vancouver South had been assured prior to his statement that the company involved intended to use Canadian contractors on the Canadian construction.
The second point I should like to cover, sir, concerns the whole question of the discussion of this bill in committee. There have been several individuals who have complained in this committee during the discussion, on clause 1. I suggest the hon. member for Skeena was one member who did so. This hon. member, as well as any other hon. member of this house, could have attended at the meetings of the committee discussing this bill if they so wished.
I should like to make one further point regarding the fact that representatives of Pembina Pipe Line Limited, and its subsidiary, Foothills pipe line, did not choose to attend the committee meetings. I would suggest they did not attend because these representatives were quite willing to stand on their own feet and accept their responsibilities and chances regarding this operation. I believe they are happy as a Canadian company to take their case to the Alberta conservation board and the national energy board. I am sure that this company Pembina Pipelines will be given a licence to set up a gathering system within the province of Alberta.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that one year ago another pipe line bill was before this committee in respect of Northern Pipe Line Limited, introduced by the hon. member for Kindersley. At that time our friends in the corner asked if the government of Saskatchewan was in favour of that bill. The hon. member for Kindersley replied that the government of Saskatchewan looked at the bill with favour and we heard nothing more from our friends in respect of that bill. Apparently our friends in the corner go along with anything the socialist government of Saskatchewan puts forward but do not wish to have competition in the field of by-products in Alberta. I point out to you, sir, as well as those members, that the element of competition is of vital importance to the people of 90205-6-185

Alberta. As I have said previously, this element of competition has a bearing on the determination of the price of these by-products to our farmers, the citizens of the small towns, and the local industries. This competition will determine the price of these very essential by-products, whether used as fuel or raw material by local industries.
Mr. Chairman, as the member for the constituency in which Pembina Pipe Line Limited head office is situated, I assure you that company, as a Canadian company, is not unwilling to take its chances with competition. I assure you, as a citizen of Alberta, that I should like to see the proper development of our resources. I should like to see local and secondary industries developed there to as great an extent as possible. I am sure that the people of Alberta need and hope to see foreign capital coming into our province to assist in the development of these resources. We ask only that Canadians be given an equal opportunity of participating in the financing and operation of these lines. I suggest to you that the government of the province of Alberta, although I do not agree with its policies in every regard, has certainly been successful in respect of the Alberta natural gas company, which was set up to gather gas in the province. I am sure that a similar course will be followed in regard to these by-products, if it is feasible. However, I want to suggest to you finally that if we, as Canadians, cannot accept the incorporation of this company because of the possible competition which will result, there is certainly something wrong with us, and for that reason we should accept this incorporation without further delay. I feel this will be a first step in the direction of allowing the export of some of our by-products which are now in a surplus position.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just sat down made certain references to a statement I made and I should like to quote from Hansard in this regard. I suggested I had information that this pipe line would be built through a negotiated contract with a United States contractor and that no Canadian firm would be allowed the opportunity of participating. This information was not held as a secret but was turned over to the hon. member for Bow River during a conversation between that hon. member and myself. He read certain excerpts from a letter he had which appeared to be rather inconclusive. I felt the excerpts would have been more conclusive had they been placed on Hansard.
I have been reported at page 2677 of Hansard as follows:
What is the situation in regard to the construction of the line? I feel I am being fair to the

Private Bills
sponsor of this bill, as I have informed him of the information I have at hand.
Further on I am reported as follows:
When I conclude my remarks I hope the hon. gentleman will be able to correct me as to the accuracy of my information.
I could have been corrected regarding my information at that time. It could be that the information was correct at that time and that the company has changed its policy since then.
It seems to me that some hon. members around here take the attitude that no one shall have his own ideas about anything in this house, and that no one except someone who lives in Alberta can talk about pipe lines. It is a matter that concerns the whole country and every hon. member in this house. If we want to talk about accuracy of statement, Mr. Chairman, I will refer you to Hansard of March 6, 1961. After certain references the hon. member for Bow River, as reported at page 2705 of Hansard, said:
Under subsection (d) of section 44-
He was referring to the act setting up the national energy board.
-the board must have regard to the question of financial responsibility. That will be considered. It must have regard to the financial structure of the applicant. That will be considered. It must have regard to the methods of financing the line. That will be considered. It must have regard to the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line. That will be considered.
What does the act say? It says that the board "may". There is a great deal of difference. It says that the board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, issue a certificate. At the end of the first clause it is stated that the board may have regard to the following and it goes on to mention the availability of oil or gas, the economic feasibility, the financial responsibility and all the rest of it. The word is not "must"; it is "may".
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

I wonder whether the hon. member has read Maxwell on the interpretation of statutes wherein it is stated that "may" may be interpreted as "shall", and vice versa. If he has done so, I should like to hear from him.

I know how lawyers can twist points. I know that two counsel can be put in a trial; that one can take one standpoint and the other can take the opposite one; and that both can buttress their arguments. All I know is simple language and to me "may"

is not "shall". If lawyers would start to write in simple language, it would be a great deal better for them also. We have heard a great deal about Canadian participation in this line. I tried to set the record straight in my opening remarks when I spoke on this bill. I referred to the evidence given by Mr. Burgis when, as reported at page 45 of the committee minutes of proceedings and evidence we find the following. This is with regard to a question by the hon. member for Calgary South who was inquiring as to the financing of the parent company and as to the degree of public participation in that financing. In reply Mr. Burgis said as follows:

Yes. We take the point of view that this is a relatively small line, and it would be quite usual for an oil company to build it as part of their normal operations. In terms of public financing in Canada back in 1957 our directors did offer public participation in the ownership of Hudson's Bay Oil & Gas, when there was no public clamor for ownership.
You say in 1957?
Yes.
But, what was the final result?

9.6 per cent-approximately 10 per cent-of the outstanding shares are owned by some 12,000 public shareholders.
I pointed out that you could take one interpretation from these remarks. The interpretation that seems to be taken by the members in their speeches was not the interpretation given in information I placed before this house and it has not been refuted as yet by anyone speaking on this bill. That information referred to the fact that the public participation in this issue came about through rights given to shareholders in Continental Oil and Hudson's Bay Company. These were rights to purchase shares in their wholly-owned subsidiary Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas. Prior to 1957 there was no public participation in the ownership of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas. The inference here is that there was public participation and that it came about through this indirect means.
I wonder how many shares are owned by Canadians or residents of this country in those parent companies, namely, Continental Oil and Hudson's Bay Company. I would venture to make this suggestion about the public participation in these companies- when I say "public" I refer to the Canadian public because I think that is what we should be concerned about in this House of Commons -that Canadian public participation in this parent company, would be, I would guess, and I emphasize the word "guess" because I trust that my hon. friend from Bow River may have detailed information on this matter, not more than 2 per cent to 3 per cent. I just wanted to set the record straight.

I agree with the fact that we want to export these commodities. But I say that in this forum we will let it be known that companies that are going to be incorporated in Canada, based upon our natural resources, shall take care that they are in tune with the climate of opinion prevailing in this country, and that climate is that Canadians shall have the right to participate. This is what I am talking about, namely the right to participate. I am not talking about not bottling up our resources; furthering logical and needed development; or taking by-products of which we have an excess to a market which needs them. All these are good things. But this benefit can be achieved in this new way of letting Canadians take part in these ventures.
This is the reason for my opposition to this bill. At no place in this evidence do I see any indication of a real attempt by the company to take this matter into account. All of the blather and furor cannot disguise that fact. I ask anyone to show me one place where any such evidence can be found. I therefore oppose this bill, Mr. Chairman. When I first spoke on it, I wanted to go to the committee to get the information. I have not obtained the information I wanted. On the basis of what I have been told today and from a reading of Hansard- and I read Hansard because I was not here for the full debate when the bill came up for consideration last Monday-I say that my questions have not as yet been answered. Until they are answered I oppose this bill.

I have maintained an interest in this bill ever since it was introduced. Through the medium of conversation and that of correspondence I have done my best to obtain every bit of factual information possible. I find myself now in the same position as that in which I was when the bill was introduced and in the same position as the hon. member for Vancouver South who has just spoken. I do not feel that we can pass clause 1. I am opposed to the bill in question. I am opposed to it for many reasons. In spite of the emphatic denials made by some hon. members, they have not been able to present answers to the problems which arise in the course of the passage of this bill for incorporation; and those answers should be given if it is to receive the authorization of this House of Commons and of the other place and royal assent.

I anticipated that we would obtain a great deal of information in committee. I am very, very sorry that for a considerable part of that meeting we did not have a reporter in attendance and the transcription is not complete. I think we have to emphasize this question. What does this bill mean, either through the reading of the bill, through the information that was given us in committee or that which has been given by the various members who supported the bill? Certain facts stand out. First, not only is it not denied but it is admitted by the sponsor of this bill and others that Aurora Pipe Line Company is a United States controlled company as far as the majority of its preferred and common shares are concerned. Second, it is not interested in developing any secondary industry in the province of Alberta.
It was most interesting to listen a few moments ago to the exhortation of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson in support of the bill. He pointed out his interest in the developing of secondary industry in the province of Alberta. We have it not only on the authority of the wording of the bill itself but also on the authority of Mr. Burgis, who appeared before the committee, that this company is not interested in any sale in Alberta whatsoever; it is only interested in export, and export to the lines of Continental Oil in Idaho and Montana. Of course, there is then a connection, if they wish, clear through to Chicago.
We have heard a great deal from hon. members who support this bill about Canadian ownership, Canadian development and the absolutely vital need for us not to be hewers of wood and drawers of water but to develop secondary industry.
I am not going into detail on this matter because it is well known to hon. members. Some two years ago this house incorporated a company which laid down as a priority requirement that the interests of Alberta should come first; second, the secondary industry in Alberta and then, and then only, export outside the boundaries of our country. Moreover not only is that organization the majority-wise Canadian owned and Canadian financed, or will be so financed if the plans go through, but we also know that they will not just deal with the southwestern corner of Alberta. They are interested in the entire province of Alberta and they have already signed what might be termed preliminary contracts to take up
75,000	barrels a day on an export basis if that much is available. We have this company to compare with the one we are now being asked to incorporate. This company only wishes to deal with the cream of the by-product group.
