Cream, my foot.

We are opposing this bill once again because we think it is a bad bill for Canada. We think it is a bill which is unnecessary inasmuch as another program could have been devised to accomplish the obtaining of markets for Canadian products. We think we are maintaining a consistent position

one which we have maintained over the years-and that this government, by supporting the present measure, is doing a disservice to the nation. We believe that once again, according to this measure, we are handing over substantial Canadian resources to the control of citizens from outside our country.
I notice that the hon. member for Greenwood is in his place. I should be most interested if he were to make some comments in this debate. I should be interested to hear his views as to whether the bill now before the committee is the best way to regulate the handling of the products concerned.
The Tory party while in opposition stood for Canadian development, Canadian participation and Canadian control over natural gas and its distribution. But since it took office there has been a complete reversal, a capitulation by the government to the United
Private Bills
States interests about which they complained so bitterly while in opposition. When this government took office they did not continue the view which they had expressed with regard to pipe lines while in opposition. They appointed a commission to try to get off the hook, but when the commission reported on the trans-Canada pipe line the report showed to what extent the interests of the nation had been sold out to United States buccaneers and certain budding millionaires in our own country. Now the position taken by the Conservative party is that even in connection with a small, short, tiny pipe line we cannot have public ownership or Canadian participation. That is a far cry from what was said with regard to the great trans-Canada pipe line. In debates on this subject on former occasions-I did not quote these references in my speech on the last occasion-the leader of the Conservative party of the day put forward the position taken by that party when he said this about the attitude of the government as recorded in Hansard for 1956 on page 2181:
This is the only place to do so and this is the opportunity to declare our economic independence of the United States. This is the time to plan to make full use of the resources which God has given us.
The hon. gentleman went on to say on the same date:
No matter how friendly any other nation may be I submit it is our duty as representatives of the people of Canada to follow a course which will assure Canada's economic as well as political independence. That course is not served by the resolution now presented to us.
I submit that that course is not served by the passage of the bill which is now under discussion in this committee. The pipe line in question is owned in the main by United States corporations which were involved in the transactions surrounding the trans-Canada pipe line.
I am pleased to see, however, that there seems to be at least a small indication of independence from the other side as was exemplified by the statement we heard today and the statements made on a former occasion by the hon. member for Vancouver South. We welcome his intervention in this debate. We think parliament would be better served if members on the opposite side sometimes gave us a little greater indication that they were exercising independent judgment and not a collective party judgment on this or other issues.
I think there is much to be answered in this debate. I wonder why the hon. member who sponsored this bill cannot give us some clear explanation as to why a capitalization of $10 million should be needed to build half a mile of pipe line. That is one of the strangest

Private Bills
things I have ever heard, that you need $10 million capitalization in order to make a $15,000 outlay. This is a preposterous proposition. It is an insult to parliament and to hon. members of this committee to ask that we rubber stamp a measure which provides $10 million capitalization for a $15,000 expenditure. I wonder what this pipe line is going to be made of, because the capitalization works out to $3,784 per foot of pipe line? Perhaps it will be gold-plated but I do not think even if it were it would cost that sum.
What does this company take us for? Why does the company want all this money? Do not tell us it is under the control of the national energy board because that is not true. What is under the control of that board is an assessment as to whether this company should have a licence to export through its half-mile of pipe line.
What about building the pipe line?

It is not going to require $10 million to build it. Surely, my hon. friend does not suggest that. The national energy board will not have control over all the other powers this company seeks to have vested in it.
What would we say about the control the government could exercise over the railway companies of Canada if they presented to parliament a couple of dozen bills or perhaps one omnibus bill which placed under the control of parliament only a half-mile of railway line connecting the railway lines between each of the provinces? That is what this company in effect, is endeavouring to do. If the railway companies were to do what I suggested in that illustration it would destroy the control of parliament over the railway system of Canada because parliament would be given control over only a few miles of railway track on provincial boundaries.
I do not know why this company chose to build a half-mile of pipe line. I do not know why it did not choose to build an even smaller one. All it wants to do is dump products over the border. Perhaps the company thought the survey of the system would not be too accurate.
The company asks to build a mere halfmile of pipe line but once the company is incorporated-if that should happen-it will have the authority given it by parliament to build pipe lines within Manitoba. Parliament will have no jurisdiction over what the company does in Manitoba, provided it does not cross a boundary. The company could build pipe lines in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and parliament would have no control. The company could build pipe

lines throughout western Canada with its $10 million capitalization and parliament would have no control, provided the pipe lines did not cross a provincial boundary.
The company is seeking wide powers in this bill. If passed, this measure will give the company not only the power to build pipe lines in half of the nation but will, under the provisions of clause 6, give the company power to build pipe lines for the transmission and transportation of oil and other liquid hydrocarbons and:
(a) within Canada in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia and in the Yukon and Northwest Territories and outside Canada construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold, develop, operate, maintain, control, lease, mortgage, hypothecate, create liens or other security upon, sell, convey or otherwise dispose of and turn to account any and all extraprovincial and/or international pipe lines and all appurtenances relative thereto for gathering, transmitting, transporting, storing and delivering of any natural or artificial gas and oil or any products or by-products thereof or any of them-
That is a lot of power for a company with half a mile of pipe line. The company could go all over Alberta gathering products under the powers sought in this bill. The company wants to build only a half-mile of pipe line, on the surface of it, but that is not all we are asked to rubber stamp. This will be one of the smallest pipe lines in Canada in terms of length.
What else does the company seek? Under the provisions of clause 6 the company seeks power to:
-own, lease, sell, operate and maintain aircraft and aerodromes for the purpose of its undertaking-
I do not know what the company will do with aerodromes in relation to a half-mile of pipe line. I have not the foggiest notion what the company proposes to do with all these powers. This is, apparently, an insignificant company. We let it go to the national energy board. Will they O.K. aerodromes and airplanes?
Not satisfied with that, the company also seeks power to:
*-own, lease, operate and maintain inter-station
telephone

With a half-mile of pipe line one would think one could shout from one end of the line to the other and be heard. I continue:
-teletype and telegraph communication systems and, subject to the Radio Act-
I thank the company for that concession.
-and any other statute relating to radio, own, lease, operate and maintain interstation radio communication facilities-
It is a wonder the company does not want television facilities.
It may do better than the C.B.C. at that.

Someone says, "It may do better than the C.B.C." Someone else wants them to have television facilities. I do not know why the company requires telephone, teletype and telegraph communication systems and aerodromes and airplanes.
The Bomarc?

I do not imagine the company would waste its money on useless contraptions. I imagine this company will spend its money very carefully.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at six o'clock I was saying that this company, which intends to build a pipe line only half a mile in length, certainly seems to want tremendous powers. It is to be given the power to operate aerodromes, to maintain aircraft, to establish telephone systems, teletype and telegraph communication systems and a host of other powers. But this tiny company, this most insignificant of all pipe lines in relation to its length, is not satisfied merely with having the power to operate pumping stations, terminals, storage tanks, aircraft and aerodromes, etc.
In order, I presume, to facilitate the construction of this tremendous project and undoubtedly in view of the countless number of employees that will be necessary to construct and to operate this half mile of pipe line, the company is asking parliament and my hon. friends opposite to rubber stamp- I think they are rubber stamping it-a provision which will allow the company to purchase, hold, lease, sell, improve, exchange or otherwise deal in real property. They may subdivide this real property into building lots and generally lay the same out into lots, streets and building sites for residential purposes. Apparently they are going to erect a city somewhere along this half mile of pipe line. They may construct streets on this real property and necessary sewerage and drainage systems and build upon the same for residential purposes or otherwise and supply any buildings so erected-
I wonder whether the hon. member would answer a question.

It is all right for the C.C.F. to do it.

I challenge the hon. member who has sponsored this bill to clean up this atrocity, to delete certain provisions of this monstrosity. Instead of the sponsor of the bill asking that this company be given the power to be a founder of cities and operator of airports, let him at least ask parliament for what he claims the company is seeking, namely, the authority to build half a mile of pipe line. After this company with its huge capitalization gets these tremendous powers it will have been clothed by parliament with the power to do all these things and I suggest that it is a disgrace; that we should not allow it and that the bill should be amended by deleting these provisions. We are being asked to approve powers to establish metropolitan areas, if you like, to build new cities, if you like. There is no limit provided in the bill, and after they have built all these houses they can lease or sell them upon such terms and subject to such conditions as appear requisite, either to their employees or to others.

Not only are we being asked to incorporate a pipe-line company but we are being asked to give the company the authority to commence housing projects, operate air lines, telephone systems, teletype and telegraph communication systems and countless other things.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Did he ever have the occasion to incorporate a company under the provincial laws of Saskatchewan by using the services of a lawyer who was worthy of his salt? If he has done so he will know that the terms are broad in any incorporation.

They may be broad and perhaps they are so broad that we should deal with them. There were 693,000 unemployed in the last count and there will be another count soon. Here is the answer to the question of unemployment: we are going to build a half mile of pipe line. If the government would build these aerodromes and other things perhaps it would be of some assistance.

Oh, oh.

I am in good company when I use that phraseology. I travel in the same company as the Prime Minister except that he has changed, he thinks it is fine now. Instead of condemning this atrocity he is now promoting it. He is promoting it and I suggest that he should be condemning it on every

There is a war of Alberta in the house.

The hon. member talks about unemployment and about trade, but he also talks against this bill. I should like to ask him if he wishes to keep this great natural resource in western Canada landlocked. Does he wish to preserve it for posterity or does he wish to market it today? There will be a time when we have another form of energy and the same thing will happen to gas and oil as happened in regard to coal not very many years ago.

Never mind making remarks about people, just answer the question.

We are very much in favour of obtaining adequate markets for the surplus products of the petroleum industry, but we think it is the duty of parliament to bring about the incorporation of pipe line companies which will export these products in such a way as to bring the greatest possible advantage to the Canadian nation. Mr. Chairman, rising once again to speak in reference to this matter, I should like to say that if any member feels there are serious questions that have not been answered I will endeavour to answer them. I am not going to take very long because I am the last one who would want to be accused of talking out his own bill. Certainly if there are any serious and honest questions, I will endeavour to answer them. I will assure every member of this committee that if there are questions which I cannot answer there are men who are connected with this company who will endeavour to supply the information.
It does seem to me, whether we like it or not, that the group in the corner have made up their minds that they are going to talk out this bill. I appeal to their intelligence. I have listened to the member for Vancouver East and have a lot of respect for him. He asked some serious questions this 90205-6-186
afternoon because he was seriously interested. I hope, in the same serious vein, that I can answer those questions.
I see the member for Assiniboia packing his papers and books. I hope he will remain with us long enough, now that he has finished his speech, to listen to some of the serious remarks that I have to make.
One of the questions that has been asked in this debate is, why is it necessary to come to parliament? Maybe it is my fault for not having answered this question before, but I thought I had. I will endeavour tonight to make this clear. Why is it necessary to come to parliament to ask for incorporation? I trust the members will bear with me when I go through the technical law in this regard, because it is very difficult to make an argument of this type. I am not appealing to emotion but to reason. I am appealing to reason based on the law of this country. If I am wrong, I trust that some hon. member will rise in his place tonight and correct me.
I should like to refer to section 25 of the energy board act, but before I do so I would refer to the fact that we are building one half a mile of pipe line. I should like to mention two points in that regard; first, why must we come to parliament? After I answer that question my second proposition will deal with the reasons for setting out the terms of incorporation as they have been set out. I am sure my friend from Assiniboia, who has a tremendous sense of humour, will bear with me while I read from the articles of incorporation of the Northern Pipe Line Company, and show that the one thing we missed-television-was included in the Saskatchewan bill.
Let us go back to my first point; why do we have to come to parliament? When the National Energy Board Act was passed, which incorporated some of the old pipe-line bill sections including section 25 to protect the Canadian public and the companies by making sure that equity was-I am sorry to see my friend from Assiniboia leaving. I am glad to see him return.

I rise on a point of order. I am listening with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member. I have an engagement tonight which I made a month ago. I must keep this engagement and I am already late. My hon. friend said he would be brief but I understand he has more to say.
I have been talking for only two minutes.
I regret very much that I will not be able to hear the hon. member.

This is one thing that should be noted. It is the first time we have been

invited to a political meeting in the House of Commons by the hon. member for Assini-boia. However, let us get down to brass tacks. These good orators from the C.C.F. leave; and this applies not only to members from the C.C.F. I noticed the other day that another good orator left as soon as he had made his point and made the press. I should like to emphasize the press. That is important for some members. Let us get back to the matter under discussion.
I rise on a question of privilege. I believe the hon. member is referring to me.
May I end this argument right now, Mr. Chairman. I had no thought of referring to my good friend from Vancouver South. I want to say that I am really sorry that he even thought I might have done so.
Are you thinking about the Prime Minister?

I want to come back, if you will bear with me, Mr. Chairman, for a few minutes to the question of the National Energy Board Act. Section 25 reads as follows:
(1) No person, other than a company, shall construct or operate a pipe line.
I want you to take heed. Everybody has been seeking facts.
(l)	No person, other than a company, shall construct or operate a pipe line.
Then it goes on to say what kind of pipe line. Let us see the definition of company. A company means, under these circumstances, as follows:
(c) "company" means a person having authority under a special act to construct or operate pipe lines;
That is the reason we are here tonight, and have been before parliament on several occasions asking for incorporation. Then, we must go to the definition of a pipe line under the same act. It is defined as follows:
(m)	"pipe line" means a line for the transmission of hydrocarbons connecting a province with any other or others of the provinces,-
Those hon. members who have given this matter careful study, and who are really conscientious in their study, will appreciate the fact that the wording of subsection (m) of section 2 is copied directly from the British North America Act. Paragraph (m) continues as follows:
-or extending beyond the limits of a province, and includes all branches, extensions, tanks, reservoirs, pumps, racks, compressors, loading facilities-
And so on. In other words-and let us get down to ordinary language-no company can

go before the energy board or do any one of the things we ask parliament to incorporate us for unless they come before this parliament and ask for a bill to incorporate the company. That is the first thing. Then as to the company, the definition of a company is one that is created by a special act and that act, Mr. Chairman, is an act of this parliament. Then it deals with pipe lines, the kind of pipe line suggested by this particular act, and exporting a particular ingredient. That is an important matter. Several hon. members have inquired why we have asked for the incorporation of a company for half a mile of pipe line. No Alberta company, Saskatchewan company or company formed in Manitoba can come before the national energy board. The company, because of the National Energy Board Act, must be a company created by a special act of parliament. That is the reason we are here.
Let us just look back to the past. I always think that history has some advantage in this regard. I am sorry that my good friend from Assiniboia has left because I want to deal with the Northern Pipe Line Company which was incorporated by chapter 61 of the statutes of Canada, 1960. If we go back, Mr. Chairman, to page 4379 of Hansard lor 1960, we shall find that the hon. member for Kindersley rose in his place in the House of Commons to sponsor a bill for the incorporation of a company that would export from the province of Saskatchewan the same products as the company of which we are asking incorporation here. The reason that he was the bill's sponsor no doubt was that he is one of our most charming members of parliament in the Conservative ranks, a man who is now 70 years of age and who had a birthday the other day. He rose in his place sponsoring a bill to incorporate a company in the province of Saskatchewan to do exactly what we are doing in the province of Alberta.
In the same circumstances?

Why do I make this point? As reported at page 4381 of Hansard of 1960, a member of the C.C.F. rose in his place. Everyone to a man, if they are sincere, would endorse the terms and conditions of the act to which I am referring and which was ridiculed by the hon. member for Assiniboia. Every term and condition was ridiculed, except one. I am sorry but I made a mistake. I do not want to lead the house astray in any particular.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You could not do so.

The hon. member for Assiniboia said that we forgot television. May I refer to page 41 of the 1960 statutes which contains the same identical section the hon.

member for Assiniboia ridiculed in reference to this company. That section was included in the bill with respect to that company and was endorsed by the C.C.F. who wish to talk this bill out. It is contained in section 6 with one clause added "or television communication facilities". He got a big laugh from the House of Commons. I am serious tonight. I do not think it is any laughing matter. I now want to read from page 4381 of Hansard a portion of the speech of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I want to express my appreciation to the hon. member from Kindersley (Mr. Han-bidge) for his fine remarks in presenting the bill to the house.
I intend to emphasize that every term and condition, with the exception of one or two things which I will mention later in this debate, was identical to what we are asking in the province of Alberta and was endorsed by the people who say they are presenting honest and straightforward arguments with no intention of talking this bill out. The quotation continues:
I should like to hear him, either when he concludes the debate or maybe this information can be made available when the bill is referred to the committee, on the reaction of the government of Saskatchewan-
There is no one in the house who needs to be reminded, even the hon. member for Vancouver South, that the government in Saskatchewan is a socialist government, the only C.C.F. experiment on the North American continent. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam wanted to know the reaction of the Saskatchewan government. May I emphasize that every term and condition that is contained in our bill is contained in the Northern Pipe Line Company bill and was endorsed by the eight members of parliament who today say they rise in their places conscientiously, without benefit of lobbyists, to oppose continually and talk out a bill merely to incorporate a company.
I have listened over the months to men in that corner of the house. I know that hon. members will agree with me tonight when I say that there is tremendous intelligence in that group. I appeal to that intelligence. I ask them to rise and to speak according to their minds and to the dictates of their hearts-
We will.

-and to say tonight that they realize that what they did when they voted for the Northern Pipe Line Company and promoted that company as a company from the province of Saskatchewan because they are C.C.F., they did believing it to be proper and of benefit to the province of 90205-6-186i

Saskatchewan. What they did on that occasion I ask this committee to duplicate on this occasion. Perhaps I may just go on reading:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Kindersley speaks now he will close the debate.
No one objected to that. Then the hon. member for Kindersley went on:

May I say a word, Mr. Speaker.
He went on to say:
With regard to the matter raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), I have to take that up with Regina. I am quite sure my hon. friend agrees with me that the government of the province is most interested in the development of the resources of the province and will do everything it can to co-operate with us in getting this company incorporated so that it will develop the oil and gas fields in Saskatchewan and promote the sale of the product.
Let us go back for a few moments. As I put the facts on the record tonight, I am speaking without any notes. I would be the last person to put any facts on the record which I did not believe to be true. I know that if my hon. friend from Assiniboia were here and were not at a political meeting he would agree with me.
However, I scanned quickly over the record in the lunch hour and found that this company was incorporated wholly with United States capital. It was wholly under United States control. Not one voice was raised by the boys in the corner, because they wanted to create every advantage for the government of the province of Saskatchewan so people would say they were doing the job well.
This is my plea to them tonight. I am sure some of these hon. members are more serious minded than they appear, and I am sure the hon. member for Peterborough will not laugh if I am completely serious about this matter. We are asking to have the same privilege in the sister province of Alberta which, because of the fate of politics, has a Social Credit government whereas Saskatchewan has a socialist government. In many ways the industries of both provinces compare one with the other. Both are agricultural provinces; both have a petroleum industry.
I come back to the Northern Pipe Line Company bill, the Minnesota pipe line system. If you analyse it, there was not one Canadian dollar in Northern Pipe Line Company. I need not go into details; I need only refer to page 4379 of Hansard, volume IV, 1960. When hon. members rise in their places in the House of Commons, as did the hon. member for Vancouver East, and say that theirs is a responsibility greater than that of the average member, I ask the hon. member to look at the record. On that date, May 31, 1960, he rose in his place in

Private Bills
the House of Commons, or remained silent- one or the other-but he endorsed everything we are asking for in the incorporation of our company.
All we from Alberta are asking is to export condensate from the Pincher Creek area. The Pincher Creek area is rather historical. Those who have lived in Alberta [DOT]-it was not my lot to be born in that province-are rather proud of Pincher Creek because it stands for two things. It is one of the great ranching areas and it is where petroleum was first found in western Canada. It created a great secondary industry, if not the first industry for those western provinces.
All we are asking is to export condensate. I have said this on three occasions, and I certainly have no malice in my heart for anyone who honestly and conscientiously, irrespective of his party, rises and opposes me in sponsoring this bill. I have asked, "What is the definition of condensate?" We have a problem in western Canada, and this is why I ask for the greatest amount of reason from the C.C.F., and I know they have a great deal. We have a surplus of wheat and we have a surplus of cattle. In fact, when I was in Japan the Japanese said, "You Canadians are unusual because your problem is that you have a surplus of everything". Now we have a surplus of petroleum.
Condensate is crude petroleum. It is the kind of product that can be properly exported from the province of Alberta or any western province to the northwest United States. I will repeat this. It can be exported to bring up our exports to 600,000 or 800,000 barrels of crude a day. In order to keep that industry healthy we are asking to build 41 miles of pipe line in the Pincher Creek area. That pipe line will be built by the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company, not by Aurora.
Hon. members have risen in their places and asked, "Why are they not building the 41 miles of pipe line?" I have read the statement which gives the reason the half-mile must be built by a particular company.
As a sponsor of the bill and of the company, which is a Canadian company, I have set out the facts. We have nothing to hide. Surely no one will rise in his place and say that we created the law. When we sponsor a bill that concerns any industry, even if it be in relation to a United States company, that company must abide by the law. That is the reason we must come to parliament to create a company for half a mile of pipe line. The 41 miles of pipe line, if and when this charter is granted and if and when the national energy board and the Alberta oil and gas

conservation board approve it, would be built by the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. This would be to the benefit of people who need employment in the province of Alberta.
I come now to the crux of the question. We are asking to do what everyone in their right senses realizes has to be done in order to get rid of our crude. We are right up to our ears in crude, in the province of Alberta, and we want to export it to the northwest United States. Hon. members will recall that we were criticized by the Social Credit government because we did not do it sooner. I am not here to argue the pros and cons of this matter, but we are asking to export a commodity of which we have a great deal. I said this the other day also.
I hope I am making myself clear in endeavouring to answer every question. I hope that when I resume my seat any really serious and honest questions in the minds of any members will be asked of me. If hon. members will put their questions briefly, I will rise in my place and answer them. All I am asking is this. Here we have a petroleum industry. We are asking to export crude petroleum to the United States because we have so much, like our wheat, our cattle and our uranium. We are asking this so we can create an industry that will give employment.
Hon. members from all parties in this house have talked about unemployment, particularly those members in whom I have a great deal of pride because they have risen from the ranks of labour. I have laboured myself. These hon. members have said they want to help people who are unemployed. Surely, to keep an industry healthy in a province, to build pipe lines and export when we have so much of the commodity will create employment. When you create an industry that will help our imbalance of trade with the United States, surely that is the only answer we have to unemployment.
If these hon. members are honest and sincere-and I am going to listen very carefully to what is said tonight-in what they say about solving the unemployment problem, I say to them with all the sincerity I can muster that if we are to reduce unemployment in the province of Alberta we must keep our petroleum industry healthy.
I would draw their attention to one thing. They talk about United States capital. Last week, according to the Calgary Herald and the Alberta newspapers, the Rocky View News and the North Hill News, which are newspapers published in Calgary, a $20 million processing plant for by-products went up within a few miles of Calgary. I believe every dollar of that $20 million was from the United States, but I believe every man who walks into the door when the

plant is open will be a Canadian taking his place at work, so that he may live in dignity with his family. I get sick when I hear lip service being paid to the plight of the unemployed. In your hearts you know, you people over there do want full employment but, really, you pay lip service to the idea because what really concerns you is political expediency. Members may accuse me of talking out my own bill, but I cannot sit in my place-I cannot be like those who have been trained longer in parliament than I-and listen to the abuse to which I was subjected this afternoon. It was said that it was a disgrace to bring in a bill which would mean the export from Alberta of a commodity which we have in such surplus. Natural gas is like wheat or any other product which we must sell to survive.
This is no time for joking. The man who has striven to be the leader of the new party in Canada stood in his place tonight and ridiculed proposals along lines which he himself had endorsed one year ago when they related to his own province. For the sake of his own political expediency he endorsed his own proposals at that time because, as he said on the platform, the old parties, the Liberals and the Conservatives, had done nothing for this country. I believe the Liberals and the Conservatives have done a lot for this country, as we all realize if we consider its development since confederation. All this has been accomplished under the Conservatives and Liberals.
Let us return to clause 6. A clause similar in every way was included in the measure respecting the Northern Pipe Line Company which hon. members in the C.C.F. group endorsed. No wonder they look serious. No wonder they are quiet in their places.
Not serious, but bored.

If members of that group are bored they should have seen the reaction when they were speaking. I hope those hon. members will bear with me. I know that in their hearts they are conscious of what they would like to do, but because of considerations of political expediency it is apparent what they will do. They will talk out this bill for development.
That is not true, Eldon.

I am glad the hon. member called me by my first name, even though it is not in accordance with our parliamentary procedure. Now I will read clause 6. The company may-
Within or outside Canada . .. construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire and hold, develop, operate, maintain, control, lease, mortgage, hypothecate, create liens or other security upon, sell,

convey or otherwise dispose of and turn to account any and all extra-provincial and/or international pipe lines and all appurtenances relative thereto for gathering, transmitting, transporting, storing and delivering of any natural or artificial gas and oil or any products or by-products thereof or any of them; including pumping stations, terminals, storage tanks or reservoirs and all works relative thereto for use in connection with the said pipe lines; and buy or otherwise acquire, transmit, transport and sell or otherwise dispose of and distribute natural or artificial gas and oil and any products or by-products thereof; and own, lease, sell, operate and maintain aircraft and aerodromes for the purpose of its undertaking, together with the facilities required for the operation of such aircraft and aerodromes; and own, lease, operate, and maintain inter-station telephone, teletype, and telegraph communication systems and, subject to the Radio Act and any other statute relating to radio, own, lease, operate and maintain interstation radio communication facilities;
Every one of the provisions included in this clause was included in the bill which was supported by the hon. member for Assini-boia and his friends. Let us ask a simple question: why are these things included here? As one hon. member said tonight-I do not remember who it was-when you are incorporating a company you must make its powers wide enough to take care of any difficulties which may arise. I may say that I practised law in Saskatchewan, and I had a great deal of respect for the attorney general of that province at that time. When we incorporated companies, all these powers were included in the articles of incorporation. Why make funny speeches? How can members practise socialism in one province and then give lip service to something entirely different outside the province?
Now we come to the capital structure of the Northern Pipe Line Company. It is stipulated that the capital stock of the company shall consist of just two million common shares with a nominal par value, and 200,000 preferred shares of par value of $100 per share. The capital structure is thus greater than that of Aurora pipe lines, but every company which is incorporated always has a greater capital structure than is necessary for its immediate objects, and all of its powers are wide enough to cover various subjects. That is part of the incorporation. It is part of company law. An hon. member may rise in his place and say: why do lawyers do this, that and the other? But I say: if anyone of you is sick, to whom does he turn? He turns to a doctor. Similarly, anyone who needs legal advice about incorporating a company turns to his lawyer.

A basic distinction between socialists and Tories is that socialists believe when they have made an error there is no sense in compounding it by making another. The hon. member's legal lecture dealt with his own interpretation of the subject. I place little reliance on his teaching ability because of his capacity for substituting one word for another and altering their meanings. I refer to his references to "shall" and "may" with which I shall deal later, if hon. members wish.
As reported at page 2705 of Hansard of March 6 the hon. member in his remarks dealt with the structure of the national energy board and the act under which it operates. He said in effect that in 1959 parliament passed the National Energy Board Act giving the board certain responsibilities and therefore we should have faith in the board in carrying out its responsibilities and give rapid and easy passage to the bill before us so the company could appear before the board.
I shall not quote the hon. gentleman's remarks in full but he made reference to sections 10, 27 and 44 of the National Energy Board Act. I shall not quote these sections nor the hon. member's remarks concerning them. I may be guilty of oversimplification in saying that he said that section 10 sets out that the board is a court of record, that section 27 deals with the granting of licences or certificates and that section 44 deals with the responsibility of the board relating to inquiring into the corporate structure of applicants. If I am wrong in my interpretation the hon. member for Bow River can correct me.
The hon. member said, in effect, that this board established by parliament had vested in it certain responsibilities and therefore we should place reliance on the ability of the board to carry out its responsibilities in the best interests of Canada.
The hon. member for Bow River dealt with section 25, in part III of the act, during the short course of law that he gave us gratuitously a while ago. Of course, being a layman in this field, I must grope my way rather

Private Bills
blindly and obviously cannot be as glib as the hon. member for Bow River in this regard. I will have to take the words as I understand them. In any event, the hon. member quoted section 25 (1) as follows:
No person, other than a company, shall construct or operate a pipe line.
Then he referred to the interpretation section which tells us what a company is and said that section 25 was the reason a private bill had to be introduced. Sections 25, 26 and 27 deal with all sorts of things but the key part is that no person, other than a company, shall construct or operate a pipe line. The bill now before us seeks to give authority to a company, as defined in the National Energy Board Act, to construct or operate a pipe line and, specifically, to construct or operate half a mile of pipe line. That is all that is being dealt with in this particular instance. If they spent the whole $10 million capitalization on building that pipe line it might provide some employment because they would be spending at the rate of about $4,000 a foot, but I do not think that is what they are going to do. In any event, I wonder whether or not this a matter which has been considered, whether or not the national energy board under its authority has done so under similar circumstances and whether or not this would not be the proper course to follow if this company sought only to build half a mile of pipe line and did not at some time in the future seek to engage in all these other activities involved in the building of homes, airports and all those other things found in the bill which the hon. member for Assiniboia indicated it was their intention to do.
Let us see what section 49 of the National Energy Board Act says. It reads as follows:
The Board may make orders exempting lines or parts of lines, not exceeding in any case a length of 25 miles, from any or all of the provisions of sections 25 to 28.
What does section 25 say? It says that no person other than a company incorporated by private act shall construct or operate a pipe line, but the board can waive that provision and can say that a company that does not have to be incorporated by private act can proceed to engage in this sort of thing. When we are given references to and interpretations of the statute by hon. gentlemen who are learned in the law, I for one expect them, especially if they are going to appeal, as some of them have, on the basis of emotionalism and not on the basis of sense or logic, to give us all of the law and point out that here is another possibility which has not been foreseen.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, is this a dissertation on the energy board or is it a debate on the Aurora Pipe Line Company?

If I may be heard on the point of order, Mr. Chairman, in listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Bow River I thought the discussion concerned the Northern Pipe Line Company which was established last year and has nothing to do with this measure.

I should like to speak to the point of order if I may. The hon. member knows as well as I do that I drew that analogy because someone rose and wanted to know the facts about the capital structure. I pointed out that the capital structure of that company established in a socialist province was identical with that of Aurora Pipe Line Company. That is the reason the analogy was drawn. The hon. member knows it, I know it, and everybody knows it.

If I may say another word on the point of order before you rule, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bow River has now substantiated my position and in effect I think he is asking you to rule that there is no point of order. I was dealing with the National Energy Board Act for the precise reason that other members who preceded me had dealt with it. Specifically, the hon. member for Bow River quoted section after section of that act. I think there is no point of order.

Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we have before us a bill that is of some importance to the province of Alberta and we are frittering away our time. My friend loves to do so and he wants to talk out the bill, but we are not dealing with the bill. We are dealing with inconsequential matters that are on the fringe of the bill and I respectfully suggest that the hon. member be called to order.

I am very sorry and I apologize to you, Mr. Chairman, and to the committee for engaging in these remarks on the side. You must admit that they were tempting. I wish that more hon. members would be like him and would have

that independence of mind, depth of conscience and clarity of thought that would allow them to take a stand similar to that of the hon. member for Vancouver South with regard to this bill and, incidentally, with regard to other bills. Some of the statements have been made almost on the assumption by the speakers that it was a government bill, when everybody in the house should know that, as a private bill, the government is not involved in it in the slightest degree.

-the party whip was in no way involved in the decisions that are taken by hon. members in the private members' hour. There is no party whip on this bill. All members are entitled to speak on this bill as they think right and proper.

Is it a proper implication that when the party whip is around, in regard to government legislation, there is no independence of thought in the ranks of the 200 members? That hon. member made remarks regarding Canadian ownership and control. He read excerpts from the proceedings of that committee. I do not wish to belabour the point by reading them again but I point out that they are available to anyone wishing to read them. He did point out that one of the answers given by Mr. Burgis was not a factual statement. Mr. Burgis did not tell a falsehood. He did not tell the whole truth but phrased the truth in such a way that it led members of that committee into the belief that shares had

been offered to the Canadian public, although there was no public clamour tor ownership. The member for Vancouver South pointed out quite clearly and honestly that this was not the case. He pointed out that not one share had been offered to the Canadian public, and I believe that is the key to this whole consideration.
Let us refer to some of the remarks made by the member for Bow River in regard to Canadian ownership and participation. One of the extensive arguments that we receive from members on the government side of the house is that we have a national energy board with certain responsibilities, one of which is to see that there is a certain amount of Canadian participation in a particular company. The impression is left that the national energy board will protect Canadian interests and that if there is not a sufficient amount of Canadian ownership of these pipe line companies the board will not grant a certificate. I think that is also the implication of many of the remarks which have been made. Let us see if that is precisely what the National Energy Board Act says. The relevant portion is section 44, and this has been distorted somewhat by my hon. friend for Bow River. Section 44 provides that the board "may" do certain things. This is a permissive word, not a mandatory one regardless of how the hon. member for Bow River substitutes meanings. Section 44 provides that the board may, subject to the approval of the governor in council, do certain things. We find that the government does have a finger in this control. The board is not an agent of the government, but we find a degree of government control which makes sure that the board carries out what it is supposed to do and does not stray too far from Tory philosophy, whatever that might happen to be from day to day. The board may issue a certificate in respect of a pipe line or an international power line if it is satisfied as to certain conditions.
Are you reading now or just talking?

I propose to read section 44(d):
-the financial responsibility and financial structure of the applicant, the methods of financing the line and the extent to which Canadians will have an opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line.
That does not in any way say that the extent of participation shall be 10 per cent, 2 per cent, 50 per cent or, and I believe Mr. Burgis mentioned this figure, 9.6 per cent. This section merely suggests that the national energy board may have regard to the extent to which Canadians will have an

opportunity of participating in the financing, engineering and construction of the line. Those are the powers given to the national energy board to ensure Canadian participation in pipe lines. Presumably this law, introduced by this government, has some connection with a paragraph in the speech from the throne this year which reads as follows:
You will be invited to consider means by which to encourage a greater participation by Canadians in the ownership and control of industry and resources in Canada.
That is wonderful, and that is from the speech from the throne. To make it official I might say I have the record, another piece of fiction, but, something which Tory members hold up as containing the truth.
The new testament?
Yes, the new testament and I find five specific items in this "new testament"-what a blasphemous reference that is-which are false.

Speaking to a point of order, the hon. member in the exuberance of his verbosity is calling the speech from the throne a piece of fiction. He referred to a pamphlet as another piece of fiction. I take it he meant the first was also fiction and, if so, he should withdraw that remark.

If the hon. member for Medicine Hat has come to that conclusion, then I can in no way account for his interpretation of what the speech from the throne meant. I will tell him that the government has as yet not lived up to the speech from the throne, nor has it lived up to any speech from the throne that has been put forward by this government since it has been in office.

speechtext: Order. I regret to tell the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to speak to this bill because I want to support it with all the force and energy that I have at my command.
As a preamble to what I have to say, I want to inform the committee that this pipe line from Pincher Creek to the boundary line is mostly in my riding of Macleod. We are tremendously interested in that area in the development of industry, exports and markets for these surplus hydrocarbons. For those who know very little about the gas and oil business, perhaps I might be pardoned if I just take a moment to say that when natural gas comes out of the ground, on the average 90 per cent in Alberta is wet gas; the other 10 per cent is dry gas. That wet gas must be scrubbed and separated. In that separation,

you take out the methane, the ethane, the propane, the butane, the pentane and the sulphur dioxide. The only natural gas that is put through the pipes to Ontario and the United States, in the large 36" pipes, is the methane gas. A market must be found for the other by-products of the gas industry. It is with those by-products and their markets that this bill deals, as they relate to the southwestern part of Alberta.
I want to say this. You cannot sell methane gas unless you take care of the by-products. The conservation board in the province of Alberta requires that these products either be marketed successfully but not wasted; they must be conserved. What is happening now in the B.A. gas field southeast of Pincher Creek is that by-products are being pumped back down into the ground for conservation. What these people want in order to operate economically, to cover their costs, to develop new fields, to increase the size of the industry, to have development, and to give employment-in order to do all these things that we are all hopeful that our industry will be able to do-is to find markets for these by-products. That is what this bill has set out to do. That is why we have been behind it. That is what we are searching for. We are hoping to find markets for these products.
We are splitting hairs when we talk about ownership and a number of problems like that. After all, I have every confidence that the people behind Aurora Pipe Line Company will give maximum consideration to Canadian participation. I believe that these people, deep down in their hearts, want Canadian participation. They want the good will of the Canadian people and may I say that they are out to assist in every way possible to develop industry in western Canada.
There is one other point I wish to make. The B.A. Oil Company, operating seventeen miles south and east of Pincher Creek, is now distributing well over 50 per cent of the natural gas which is being piped to Ontario to warm Ontario homes. That is something to ponder and consider. I refer to the fact that out of that one small area you have this tremendous volume of natural gas. Just west of Pincher Creek some ten or 12 miles, another field is being developed by Shell Oil Company and they also will have their problem of marketing by-products.
Before you can strip out methane and put it through the pipelines to California or export it to Ontario you must find a method by which to take care of those by-products. It is the problem of a market for those byproducts that this Aurora Pipe Line Company seeks to solve. That is why I, as member of parliament for Macleod riding, feel it my
Private Bills
duty to rise in my place and do everything I possibly can to support this bill.
For the life of me I cannot see how a small and, I may say, vocal group in the far corner of the chamber can continue to filibuster a measure such as this one which is in the best interests of the people of that area. It would give employment. I may say that the other pipe lines which are being built through the Crowsnest pass down to Kingsgate and in that direction are giving a tremendous impetus and employment to the people of that area. But before this pipe line can properly operate from Savanna Creek, from the Shell plant at Pincher Creek and from these other areas we must, above all, find a market for these surplus products. There is no room, when starting a new field to pump them back down into the ground. In other words, at present the only place where by-products can be disposed of is in the ground. So I say that in order for these companies to operate economically, they must have a market for these surplus products.
There is no other way in which to deal with them than to sell them to whomever we can sell them and wherever we can find any market for them. They must be shipped by pipe line. They cannot be transported otherwise; except in the case of sulphur, they must be put through a pipe line. That is the most economical way of transporting them. Then, by fractional distillation they are made into some 10,000 different products. For those hon. members who are not familiar with the oil industry let me say that from these by-products about which we are talking here this evening there can be made approximately
10,000	products that serve the needs of mankind. This number of products can be made from these hydrocarbons that are taken from the wet gas as it comes from these fields.
Again, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I do not want to take up any more time in discussing this bill. However, I hope that those in the far corner will co-operate regardless of the fact that they may think sufficient consideration has not been given to Canadian participation. I believe that is a matter which will be taken care of properly. The bill is not different from the act which has been passed in Saskatchewan; and I am sure that Alberta is in a much more serious condition with respect to the marketing of these by-products than Saskatchewan ever dreamed of being. I therefore hope that those in the far corner, like all other members of the House of Commons, will rise to the occasion and give approval to this bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am afraid we are involved in two or three questions in connection with this bill. To answer that question, I would have to go into what results the oil industry has produced in the field of employment and how much has been taken over by automation.
Very few men run a very large industry in Ontario. I do not think there is very much difference between the operation of the oil industry in Ontario and in the west. Many red herrings have been drawn into this debate. The unemployment question is the last in a long series of such red herrings. If we were going to dig a second trans-Canada pipe line with a pick and shovel I would support the bill on the basis of solving the unemployment problem, but to dig half a mile of pipe line-and I do not care where it starts or ends-is not going to solve the unemployment problem when we consider that we have
600,000	or 700,000 unemployed people.
We are faced with another problem. Many hon. members of this house are not the least bit interested in honesty; they are not the least bit interested in the over-all economy of the country; they are not particularly interested in the employment or the unemployment picture. speechtext: We heard this afternoon and this evening one hon. member saying one thing and another hon. member quoting from the same document and saying something else. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The matter is very simple. I think everybody agrees that we are not particularly concerned with this half-mile of pipe line that is being discussed at the present time or the fact that it will export something like 11,000 barrels of crude oil a day. The national energy board suggests that we have an export potential of something like 800,000 barrels of oil a day. What we are now suggesting is that these products must and can be held in Canada and used in Canada for the development of industry in Canada.
Certainly the hon. member who asked the last question should be the last person to object to this aim because in his own part of the country he has seen, as I have seen in mine and as those in northern Quebec have seen, that the exportation of our raw materials has taken place without secondary industry ever being developed.
The previous speaker in this debate talked about developing secondary industry and industry in Canada. If we have a product in a surplus market, I am quite sure that as the price drops for that surplus product there will be an opportunity for some enterprising businessman to go into that field and start developing a secondary industry in which to use this very cheap commodity. We all know that as the demand for the commodity increases as the secondary industry develops, the price will again rise and will level itself off at a competitive price.
The national energy board was of course set up a few years ago when the members of this government believed we should be working towards developing industry in Canada

for Canadians and utilizing our natural resources to the greatest degree. The national energy board was set up for this purpose. We are now being asked to set up a company which will, in my opinion, contravene the aims that we had when we set up the national energy board. We are being asked to set up a fully-fledged company whose only purpose is to drain off and funnel out of Alberta these condensates, these high calibre oil and gasoline bearing commodities. We are channelling these materials into the United States, where they will go into the Chicago area and secondary industry development will take place.
We suggest that this secondary industry development can take place in Canada. It can be done by Canadians and used for the benefit of all Canadians. I agree that the hon. members from Alberta are probably unhappy that this was not done immediately, because it would mean an immediate draining off of some of these surplus products- and I am told they are surplus products-to the United States and a few dollars would come back to the Alberta oil fields. Of course, this would be of some advantage to Alberta. But is it not also true that when we carried our coal off to some other place we obtained some advantage out of it? It was certainly true in northern Ontario when we exported our pulp and paper in its raw form into the United States. We obtained some advantage out of it, but how much more advantage would we have obtained if we had established a secondary industry there? That secondary industry could have been established in our area. We would have obtained a great deal more advantage from it for our community and for the country in general.
I think those hon. members from Quebec in particular should be very much interested in this, because they have seen exactly the same thing happening in regard to their northern iron industry. The iron ore goes down through Seven Islands, where we could have steel plants larger than anything on the North American continent, and goes into Pittsburgh where it helps United States development.
If we are going to be only an adjunct to the United States, this is perfectly all right. However, I want to see secondary industry in Canada. This can come about only if we take advantage of whatever natural resources we have. In my opinion they are not the God-given right of those people in Alberta only, but they belong to the whole Canadian economy. We should also start some of these benefits flowing into the eastern markets, because while westerners may talk about a surplus of gasoline and oil, there is no surplus
Private Bills
in the rest of Canada. We export 6| million barrels and we import 6| million barrels. I do not see where there is any great surplus when one looks at the Canadian economy as a whole.
It seems to me that some of these westerners had better forget about the buccaneers they met when the trans-Canada pipe line come into being and should start thinking Canadian rather than in the buccaneer manner. It is all right to carry the bible under your arm, to preach about all the natural resources we have and how wonderful everything is going to be under the free enterprise system. But it has not been too good in these areas where this type of development has occurred. It is not only the social credit domain that has allowed exploitation on an unlimited scale in those fortunate areas where resources are abundant, but this has also been done in Ontario. I would not like to see again the exploitation that has taken place previously in Canada and which will take place if this pipe line is built.
I agree that it may seem odd to put up such a fight for such a small section of line, but it does not seem to me that it is going to be a small section of line. If an hon. member or one of his friends decided, as a person, to build this half mile of pipe line I am quite sure his exportation program would receive a thorough scrutiny from the national energy board. When this company is established, if it becomes established, I am sure it will not build merely a half a mile of pipe line. I am sure it will eventually have pipe lines running into the Yukon, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and other provinces. If this is not the case, why would they ask for a capitalization of $10 million? Why would they ask for the right to build airports? Certainly, hon. members are correct when they ask these questions, because if they listen to the story being told that all this company wants to do is to build half a mile of pipe line they are bound to say that this company does not need airfields or aeroplanes. They certainly have no need for these things unless there is a question involved of avoiding income tax, writing off assets and getting depreciation. There is no legitimate reason for having this corporation established with such a large capitalization if it does not intend to build pipe lines throughout an interprovincial area.
The initial stage of this venture calls for the draining off of the oil surplus and its transmission to the United States, but tremendous developments will probably take place. One hon. member asked tonight why something had not been done with regard to public utilities on a national basis. It is

Private Bills
not true that we do not have one of these developments. You may remember, Mr. Chairman, that only recently the Canadian government bought from the United States a pipe line which they owned lock, stock and barrel. We bought this pipe line, a pipe line which has attached to it airports and even a couple of villages. I would ask the hon. member sponsoring this measure if he can find out from the government what happened to this particular pipe line. I do not think he could find out. But we have, or at least we had, a pipe line which belonged to us, and it passed through the area which this proposed company would like to cover, in part, at least. I suggest that before setting up this elaborate company to export surplus Canadian oil we should find out what has happened to the resources of that concern.
This proposed company will export a relatively small amount in the over-all picture, perhaps less than 1 per cent of our total surplus, or the full amount available for export. Even when this pipe line is carrying its capacity load we shall only be moving one tenth of the amount which the government has indicated would be available eventually for exportation. Hon. members can stand up and talk about lawyers. It is always true, of course, that lawyers are never right and never wrong. At least, they can never be more than 50 per cent wrong because there is always one of them on each side of an argument, though between them they do not make up 100 per cent of the truth. So it is not fair to stand up and give this flexible lawyer-interpretation of the powers said to be needed by the company. I think this committee is entitled to the actual facts. If the company only intends to build half a mile of pipe line, then let this bill be withdrawn. Let us recommend here that the bill go back to the committee. Let the sponsor explain to his principals that he is not prepared to support the present measure with its large capitalization but that he is prepared to sponsor a bill calling for $15,000 to build half a mile of pipe line and to seek the necessary powers commensurate with the construction of a pipe line of this teeny-weeny length.
I think the hon. member for Bow River is not being entirely fair if he talks continually about the money it will cost to build half a mile of pipe line, while at the same time asking us to endorse the granting of powers which seem to me to be wider even than those possessed by the national energy board itself. These powers enter upon many fields. They will infringe on the responsibilities of four or five departments of government. They will enable the

company to build airports, fly aeroplanes, construct houses, transmit by radio, build highways, and, possibly, build townsites and schools. If development of this type is, indeed, envisaged, then I think we should be told, in which case I do not think there is a member in this chamber who would not oppose the incorporation of a company for these purposes. On the other hand, if the sponsor is only asking for this restricted development then I think he should make that very clear, and the verbiage which is now in the bill should be removed. I think that is a simple proposition.
I believe it should also be made clear that we in this party are not opposed to the orderly marketing of the surplus of a product, but we are of the opinion that this government must give very serious consideration to the establishment in Canada of secondary industry. Such industries do depend upon government assistance, and, I believe, can only be established with government assistance and direction. I think now is the time when we should decide if we want new secondary industry. It may sound a bit like socialism-
Are you suggesting subsidies, which would mean high tariffs?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am suggesting that if we approve bills of this type we would in effect be subsidizing the people who are going to participate financially, and they are not Canadians. It is not a Canadian company which is going to benefit. I suggest we should subsidize new secondary industries if necessary, particularly in association with the oil industry. In the United States around the city of Chicago there are important secondary industries which live off the waste not only of these condensates but the waste which come from the wastes after the gasoline has been taken out of the condensates. This is not only sulphur. I am told they make coal tar products and all types of manufactures, including aspirin, from these byproducts and distillates from the petroleum products and I suggest that if this can be done in the United States it can be done as well and cheaper in Canada.
There would be no objection then, I think, to allowing the exploitation of these finished products. It seems to me we should have learned our lesson by now. I see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Minister of Forestry are here tonight and each of them will realize the vast amount of natural resources we have sent out of this country in a raw state. They would appreciate the fact that in the next generation we must create secondary industries in our own country and foster this new development

around the industries with which we are blessed. If I am wrong somebody will correct me-
You are wrong.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But it will not be the minister from Medicine Hat because, frankly, I do not think he can tell me anything on this subject. He just asks a lot of silly questions, but there is nothing he could tell me.
He would not need to know much to tell you anything.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: And that goes for the minister from Acadia, too. I do not use the word "minister" in the sense of cabinet ministers but in the sense of people who go around the country spreading the gospel of social credit. I am surprised-

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the hon. gentleman is accusing me and the hon. member for Acadia of being Social Crediters. That is the last thing in the world we want to be. The second last thing would be a C.C.F.'er.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I apologize for injecting this note into the debate because we have not time to discuss it. I could point out the similarities but is would not accomplish anything. Those who listen will know. People will support provincially the same candidates they do federally.
It has been said that if it walks like a duck, looks like a duck and smells like a duck, in all probability it is a duck. What we have seen of the exploitation program in Alberta indicates there is a duck somewhere in the picture.
The hon. member for Bow River in his remarks raised two questions. The first was why the pipe line company should come to parliament with this bill, and the second was why we have the present terms of the bill. I am not sure that I know why the company has come to parliament. Section 25 of the National Energy Board Act sets out who may construct and operate pipe lines and states the exception. It is difficult to know why this bill should come before parliament or why the company should require capitalization of $10 million.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. We have heard this a million times. As I recall it, we have a rule against repetition. It is now five minutes to ten. I appreciate that the C.C.F. has decided to talk out this measure but we have heard this argument a million times, and at least a dozen times from the hon. member who has the floor. His needle is stuck on the record. If we could have the record changed, it would not be too bad.
Private Bills

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I have even less respect than before for the hon. member's intelligence. The hon. member raised these new points this afternoon and spent considerable time explaining them. I humbly suggest that no one has had a chance to talk more than once or twice, the hon. member and I being among those who have had. The hon. member has created confusion with his explanation concerning the $15,000 expenditure and the capitalization of $10 million. There must be an explanation for the discrepancy.
Section 34, subsection 2.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It is interesting to note-

Would the hon. member permit a question. Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the petrochemical industry of western Canada has sufficient by-products to last for
1,000	years? We could export the by-products from the entire field at Pincher Creek and have enough left from other fields for the industry to continue for a thousand years. Therefore, the hon. members opposite are not talking about stopping the growth of western Canada. They cannot attack this measure on that ground. They must in fact attack it on the basis of whether we need those byproducts in Canada. The answer is that we do not need them in Canada and should export them.
That is a simple, physical fact which does not appear to have sunk into the head of my hon. friend and until he appreciates that fact he will be arguing on completely false grounds in opposing this bill.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I noticed that the hon. member received applause for that statement. Let me tell him, through you, sir, that a similar statement was made many years ago with respect to the white pine industry in the Ottawa valley. A scientist like the hon. member came from Sweden, an expert in the white pine industry. He spent several months touring the Ottawa valley and returned to Sweden. He said that no matter how much white pine they cut in Canada, the supply would never be exhausted.
The hon. member is simply against the export of gas.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The scientist said the supply would go on forever, but now there is no white pine industry in the Ottawa valley. The hon. gentleman received applause for making a similar statement with respect to a non-renewable industry, a commodity that cannot be replaced.
Progress reported.

Business of the House BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire of the house leader what is the order of business for tomorrow and Wednesday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
There will be a slight change from what I announced on Thursday evening. The first item tomorrow will be second reading of Bill No. C-57 to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. The second item will be No. 12 on today's order paper, the motion standing in the name of the Minister of Agriculture to empower the standing committee on agriculture and colonization to continue its inquiry into the question of prices of farm machinery.
The third item which I had called, namely the army benevolent fund, I should like to postpone. If the house will give its required unanimous consent I should like instead to proceed with a motion to refer Bill No. C-71 relating to the Civil Service Act to the special committee which was appointed on Friday, the membership of which was listed today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What is the number of that item of business as it appears on the order paper?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not on the order paper because on Friday we omitted directing what should be done with that bill. There is some slight difference of opinion as to whether or not we have already referred the bill to the committee.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I was under the impression we had, as I indicated to the house leader earlier.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On Friday we resolved that a special committee be appointed to consider Bill No. C-71 and today we named the committee but we did not actually refer the bill to this committee. That is what I am talking about now.
The fourth item will be item No. 7 on today's order paper, the resolution in the name of the Minister of Labour dealing with programs of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons.
On Wednesday we will start with Bill No. C-73 which has reference to the Income Tax Act.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: With respect to the consent for which the house leader asked, we on this side are quite happy to give consent in that matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is consent to deal tomorrow with the motion to refer Bill No. C-71 to the standing committee?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. It has been established.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unless the house wishes to refer the bill tonight?

Tomorrow will be soon enough.
It being four minutes past ten o'clock, the house, adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Questions
